# Exmoor National Park

Scroll down


## Where the moor meets the sea

Towering sea cliffs, high moors, tumbling streams and deep valleys that shelter our unique Atlantic Rain forest.On Exmoor it is still possible to find tranquillity and peace as well as rediscover your sense of adventure; to catch a glimpse of wild red deer, be amazed by dark skies full of stars and explore quaint villages full of character and charm.

- [@ExmoorNP](https://twitter.com/@ExmoorNP)
- [ExmoorNP](https://facebook.com/ExmoorNP)

## Key activities

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/exmoor_exp_autumn_valley_of_rocks_2019_cf025238_final_WEB-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/enjoying/walking)

### [Walking , Activity](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/enjoying/walking)

Exmoor’s 1000km of rights of way makes for a true walker’s paradise, providing spectacular access to the rugged heritage coastline amid high open moorland, wooded combes and tumbling streams. It's a landscape that has inspired generations of poets, artists and writers.

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/North-Devon-Coast-1-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.southwestcoastpath.org.uk/itineraries/3)

### [South West Coast Path , Activity](https://www.southwestcoastpath.org.uk/itineraries/3)

Exmoor’s 60km coastline forms the first stage of the South West Coastal Path – the UK’s longest National Trail. Sometimes called the ‘Wilderness Coast’, the route journeys along high sea cliffs, remote moors, steep-sided gorges and isolated beaches.

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Keith-Trueman-credit-Star-Trails-over-Valley-of-Rocks-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/stargazing)

### [Stargazing , Activity](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/stargazing)

As Europe’s first International Dark Sky Reserve, Exmoor is one of the best places in the country for stargazing. On a clear night the Milky Way, shooting stars and thousands of glittering stars and constellations are clearly visible with the naked eye. The annual Exmoor Dark Skies Festival in October is an ideal time to experience them.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Exmoor-Pony-Foal-Porlock-Bay-lr-1200x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

What makes Exmoor special?

The story of Exmoor begins millions of years ago with the movement of tectonic plates. From that erupted the genesis of the landscape we see today: raw material that was shaped and reshaped by geological and geomorphological processes, as well as human intervention.

It’s easy to forget that Exmoor is in no small part an environment made by people. But millennia of farming, mining, fuel-making, settlement, defence and recreation have left their mark, forming the unique landscape that is now Exmoor National Park.

At just 693 square kilometres, Exmoor is one of the UK’s smallest National Parks. But what it lacks in size it more than makes up for in beauty and variety, thanks to spectacular coastline, expansive moorland, steep wooded valleys with fast flowing rivers and streams, and rolling farmland.

The value of Exmoor is not only aesthetic. From a conservation point of view, the moorlands and oak woodlands are designated internationally for the habitats and species they support. And our archaeological and cultural heritage is remarkable: new sites and discoveries are frequent in the National Park, and we enjoy a rich tradition of local art, literature, music and food.

Then there are the night skies, which really are out of this world. We’re officially an International Dark Sky Reserve, thanks to the wondrous starry roof that’s visible when the sun goes down.

## Did you know?

Exmoor has the highest coastline on the British mainland. It reaches a height of 314 metres above sea level.

# A distinctive landscape

Exmoor is a unique and very special place – a distinctive landscape shaped by generations of people who have farmed and managed the environment for thousands of years. Today it is celebrated and enjoyed for its wonderful variety of heather and grass moors, its ancient woodlands and forests, picturesque villages, dramatic coastline, magnificent herds of Red deer and native ponies, and at night the magic of its dark skies. We passionately want to see a healthy and beautiful environment thriving alongside communities and tourism. We also want to see more people from all walks of life visiting and enjoying Exmoor, and future generations continuing to be inspired by its extraordinary beauty, wildlife and history. None of this is achievable without an unwavering commitment to tackling climate change and biodiversity loss. Which is why, as part of a family of 15 National Parks encompassing some of the country’s most precious natural resources, we’re dedicated to being part of the solution and to leaving our environment in a better state than we found it for future generations.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/exmoor_exp_dark_skies_2018_exmoor_exp_dark_skies_2018__mg_8894_final_FINAL_WEB-1800x1080.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/exmoor_exp_autumn_family_2018_mg_0307_FINAL-580x580.jpg)

### Getting there

First Great Western and Cross Country rail services from London and the Midlands serve both Taunton and Tiverton Parkway stations, around a 60-minute bus journey from the National Park. The Tarka line connects Exeter to Barnstaple – a 30 minute bus ride from Exmoor.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/exmoor_exp_cycling_2018_cf021384_FINAL_WEB-580x580.jpg)

### Getting around

A number of different bus routes service the area. The nearest mainline rail stations are just outside the National Park in Taunton and Tiverton Parkway. For walkers, around 1000km of Rights of Way traverse Exmoor. The West Country Way – a national cycle route – crosses the moor and provides links with rail stations at Barnstaple, Tiverton Parkway and Taunton.

### Supporting Nature Recovery

Find out what we are doing to work together for a more nature rich future Exmoor.

### Your Natural Health Service

We want everyone to enjoy the benefits that getting out on Exmoor can have to their health and wellbeing.

[Find out more about Health and Wellbeing](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/exmoor-for-everyone/health-and-wellbeing)

![Group on Exmoor](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/__data/assets/image/0017/3464/15607745782_fc1ba43b08_k.jpg)

### Taking on the challenge of Climate Change

From planting new woodland to locking up carbon in our peatlands we're taking positive action to limit climate change and ensure Exmoor is resilient and thriving now and in the future.

[Find out more about our Climate Work](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/community/climate-action)

![tree planting bywood](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/__data/assets/image/0015/3462/IMG_0311.jpg)

### Caring for our Landscape and Heritage

Exmoor has as rich history and a landscape that tells the story of how people have lived and worked here from the Mesolithic to today.

[Explore Landscape and Heritage](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/nature-and-landscape)

![Tarr Steps in Autumn](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/__data/assets/image/0006/4020/Tarr-Steps-autumn.jpg)

### Celebrating A living landscape

Working with our communities and businesses to help keep Exmoor special.

[Find out more about Exmoor Communities and Business.](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/community)

![Withypool image on Exmoor - Andrew Hobbs](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/__data/assets/image/0026/6785/Withypool.jpg)

### A National Park for Everyone

Exmoor is a place for everyone to explore, cherish and care for.

[Find out more about enjoying Exmoor](https://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/exmoor-for-everyone)

The national park boundaries | | Location | [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") ( [South West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England")) | | Area | 692km2 (267sqmi) | | Established | 1954 | | Governingbody | Exmoor National Park Authority | | Website | [http://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/](http://www.exmoor-nationalpark.gov.uk/) | **Exmoor** ([/ˈɛksmʊər,-mɔːr/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[Play audio](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/48/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Tesco250-Exmoor.wav/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Tesco250-Exmoor.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Tesco250-Exmoor.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Tesco250-Exmoor.wav")) is loosely defined as an area of hilly open [moorland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moorland "Moorland") in west [Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset "Somerset") and north [Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon "Devon") in [South West England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England"). It is named after the [River Exe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Exe "River Exe"), the source of which is situated in the centre of the area, two miles north-west of [Simonsbath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simonsbath "Simonsbath"). Exmoor is more precisely defined as the area of the former ancient royal hunting forest, also called Exmoor, which was officially surveyed 1815–1818 as 18,810 acres (7,610ha or 76.1km2) in extent. The moor has given its name to a [National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_England_and_Wales "National parks of England and Wales"), which includes the [Brendon Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendon_Hills "Brendon Hills"), the [East Lyn Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Lyn_Valley "East Lyn Valley"), the Vale of Porlock and 55km (34mi) of the [Bristol Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Channel "Bristol Channel") coast. The total area of the Exmoor National Park is 692.8km2 (267.5mi2), of which 71% is in Somerset and 29% in Devon. The upland area is underlain by [sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") rocks dating from the [Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian "Devonian") and early [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous") periods with [Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic "Triassic") and [Jurassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic "Jurassic") age rocks on lower slopes. Where these reach the coast, cliffs are formed which are cut with ravines and waterfalls. It was recognised as a [heritage coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_coast "Heritage coast") in 1991. The highest point on Exmoor is [Dunkery Beacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkery_Hill "Dunkery Hill"); at 519 metres (1,703ft) it is also the highest point in Somerset. The terrain supports [lowland heath communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaths_in_the_British_National_Vegetation_Classification_system "Heaths in the British National Vegetation Classification system"), [ancient woodland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_woodland "Ancient woodland") and [blanket mire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanket_bog "Blanket bog") which provide habitats for scarce flora and fauna. There have also been reports of the [Beast of Exmoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beast_of_Exmoor "Beast of Exmoor"), a [cryptozoological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptozoology "Cryptozoology") [cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat "Cat") roaming Exmoor. Several areas have been designated as [Nature Conservation Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Nature_Conservation_Review "A Nature Conservation Review") and [Geological Conservation Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological_Conservation_Review "Geological Conservation Review") sites. There is evidence of human occupation from the [Mesolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesolithic "Mesolithic"). This developed for agriculture and extraction of mineral ores into the [Bronze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") and [Iron Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age"). The remains of [standing stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menhir "Menhir"), [cairns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairn "Cairn") and bridges can still be identified. The royal forest was granted a charter in the 13th century, however foresters who managed the area were identified in the [Domesday Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book"). In the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") sheep farming was common with a system of [agistment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agistment "Agistment") licensing the grazing of livestock as the [Inclosure Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inclosure_Acts "Inclosure Acts") divided up the land. The area is now used for a range of recreational purposes. ## National character area \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exmoor&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: National character area")\] Exmoor has been designated as a [national character area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_character_area "National character area") (No. 145) by [Natural England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_England "Natural England"), the public body responsible for England's natural environment. Neighbouring natural regions include [The Culm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culm_Measures#National_character_area "Culm Measures") to the southwest, the [Devon Redlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon_Redlands "Devon Redlands") to the south and the [Vale of Taunton and Quantock Fringes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_Taunton_and_Quantock_Fringes "Vale of Taunton and Quantock Fringes") to the east.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-1) ## Exmoor National Park \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exmoor&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Exmoor National Park")\] Exmoor was designated a National Park in 1954, under the 1949 [National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Parks_and_Access_to_the_Countryside_Act_1949 "National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-authority-2) The Exmoor National Park is primarily an [upland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland "Highland") area with a dispersed population living mainly in small villages and hamlets.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-4) The largest settlements are [Porlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porlock "Porlock"), [Dulverton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulverton "Dulverton"), [Lynton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynton "Lynton"), and [Lynmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynmouth "Lynmouth"), which together contain almost 40 per cent of the park's population. Lynton and Lynmouth are combined into one parish and are connected by the [Lynton and Lynmouth Cliff Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynton_and_Lynmouth_Cliff_Railway "Lynton and Lynmouth Cliff Railway").\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Exmoor was once a [royal forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_forest "Royal forest") and hunting ground, covering 18,810 acres (7,610ha),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-5) which was sold off in 1818.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-6) Several areas within the Exmoor National Park have been declared [Sites of Special Scientific Interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site_of_Special_Scientific_Interest "Site of Special Scientific Interest") due to their flora and fauna.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-glenthornesssi-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-northexmoorsssi-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-southexmoorsssi-9) This title earns the site some legal protection from development, damage and neglect. In 1993 an [environmentally sensitive area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmentally_sensitive_area "Environmentally sensitive area") was established within Exmoor.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-10) It is known as a perfect place for [stargazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_astronomy "Amateur astronomy"). In 2011, it was designated Europe's first International Dark Sky Reserve by the [International Dark-Sky Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Dark-Sky_Association "International Dark-Sky Association").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-11) ## Geology \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exmoor&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Geology")\] Main article: [Geology of Exmoor National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_Exmoor_National_Park "Geology of Exmoor National Park") Exmoor is an upland area formed almost exclusively from [sedimentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedimentary_rock "Sedimentary rock") rocks dating from the [Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian "Devonian") and early [Carboniferous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous "Carboniferous") periods. The name of the [geological period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_(geology) "Period (geology)") and [system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_(stratigraphy) "System (stratigraphy)"), 'Devonian', comes from Devon, as rocks of that age were first studied and described here. With the exception of a suite of [Triassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic "Triassic") and [Jurassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic "Jurassic") age rocks forming the lower ground between Porlock and Timberscombe and from Minehead to [Yarde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nettlecombe,_Somerset "Nettlecombe, Somerset") (within Exmoor National Park but peripheral to the moor itself),[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-13) all of the solid rocks of Exmoor are assigned to the [Exmoor Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor_Group "Exmoor Group"), which comprises a mix of [gritstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gritstone "Gritstone"), [sandstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone"), [slates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate "Slate"), [shales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shale "Shale"), [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone"), [siltstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siltstone "Siltstone") and [mudstones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudstone "Mudstone"). [Quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz "Quartz") and [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") mineralisation can be detected in outcrops and [subsoil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsoil "Subsoil").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-14) The [Glenthorne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenthorne "Glenthorne") area demonstrates the Trentishoe Member (formerly 'Formation') of the Hangman Sandstone Formation (formerly 'Group'). The Hangman Sandstone represents the Middle Devonian sequence of North Devon and Somerset.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-glenthornesssi-7) These unusual freshwater deposits in the Hangman Grits were mainly formed in desert conditions.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-exmoorgeology-15) As this area of Britain was not subject to [glaciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacial_period "Glacial period"), the plateau remains as a remarkably old landform.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-exmoorgeology-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-16) The bedrock and more recent superficial deposits are covered in part by moorland which is supported by wet, acid soil.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exmoor#cite_note-eelandscape-17) ## Geography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exmoor&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Geography")\] ### Coastline \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Exmoor&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: Coastline")\] [![Ricky peaks and cliffs topped by greenery, with a small s
